nodes.name: Theorem 1.1 (Hecke eigenform criterion)
nodes.statement: Let $f\in S_k(\Gamma_1(N))$ be a holomorphic cuspform of arbitrary weight and level. If the associated complete $L$-function $\Lambda_f(s)=\int_0^\infty f(iy)y^{s-1}\,dy$ does not vanish for $\Re(s)>\frac{k+1}2$ then $f$ is an eigenfunction of the Hecke operators $T_p$ for all primes $p\nmid N$.
nodes.statement_short: A holomorphic cuspform whose complete $L$-function has no zeros in $\Re(s)>\frac{k+1}2$ must be a Hecke eigenform.
assumptions: Let $f\in S_k(\Gamma_1(N))$ be a holomorphic cuspform of arbitrary weight and level.
the associated complete $L$-function $\Lambda_f(s)=\int_0^\infty f(iy)y^{s-1}\,dy$ does not vanish for $\Re(s)>\frac{k+1}2$
conclusions: $f$ is an eigenfunction of the Hecke operators $T_p$ for all primes $p\nmid N$

nodes.name: Theorem 1.2 (main theorem: monomial dichotomy for polynomials in automorphic $L$-functions)
nodes.statement: Fix a positive integer $n$. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $r_j$ be a positive integer and $\pi_j$ a unitary cuspidal automorphic representation of $\GL_{r_j}(\mathbb{A}_\Q)$ with $L$-series $L(s,\pi_j)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\lambda_j(m)m^{-s}$. Assume that the $\pi_j$ satisfy the generalized Ramanujan conjecture at all finite places (so that, in particular, $|\lambda_j(p)|\le r_j$ for all primes $p$) and are pairwise non-isomorphic. Let $$ R=\left\{\sum_{m=1}^M\frac{a_m}{m^s}:M\in\Z_{\ge0}, (a_1,\ldots,a_M)\in\C^M\right\} $$ denote the ring of finite Dirichlet series, and let $P\in R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ be a polynomial with coefficients in $R$. Then either $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ has a zero with real part $>1$ or $P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $D\in R$, $d_1,\ldots,d_n\in\Z_{\ge0}$.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial in automorphic $L$-functions over the ring of finite Dirichlet series either has a zero with $\Re(s)>1$ or is a monomial.
assumptions: For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $r_j$ be a positive integer and $\pi_j$ a unitary cuspidal automorphic representation of $\GL_{r_j}(\mathbb{A}_\Q)$ with $L$-series $L(s,\pi_j)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\lambda_j(m)m^{-s}$.
Assume that the $\pi_j$ satisfy the generalized Ramanujan conjecture at all finite places (so that, in particular, $|\lambda_j(p)|\le r_j$ for all primes $p$) and are pairwise non-isomorphic.
let $P\in R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ be a polynomial with coefficients in $R$
conclusions: either $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ has a zero with real part $>1$ or $P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $D\in R$, $d_1,\ldots,d_n\in\Z_{\ge0}$

nodes.name: Jacquet--Shalika non-vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: For $\pi_j$ as in the statement of the theorem, it is known (see \cite{jacquet-shalika}) that $L(s,\pi_j)$ does not vanish for $\Re(s)\ge1$.
assumptions: For $\pi_j$ as in the statement of the theorem
conclusions: $L(s,\pi_j)$ does not vanish for $\Re(s)\ge1$

nodes.name: Saias--Weingartner theorem on Dirichlet series with periodic coefficients
nodes.statement: In \cite{SW}, Saias and Weingartner showed that if $L(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\frac{\lambda(m)}{m^s}$ is a Dirichlet series with periodic coefficients, then either $L(s)=0$ for some $s$ with real part $>1$, or $\lambda(m)$ is multiplicative at almost all primes (so that $L(s)=D(s)L(s,\chi)$ for some primitive Dirichlet character $\chi$ and finite Dirichlet series $D$).
nodes.statement_short: Degree-1 case: a Dirichlet series with periodic coefficients either vanishes somewhere in $\Re(s)>1$ or essentially has an Euler product.
assumptions: $L(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\frac{\lambda(m)}{m^s}$ is a Dirichlet series with periodic coefficients
conclusions: either $L(s)=0$ for some $s$ with real part $>1$, or $\lambda(m)$ is multiplicative at almost all primes (so that $L(s)=D(s)L(s,\chi)$ for some primitive Dirichlet character $\chi$ and finite Dirichlet series $D$)

nodes.name: Davenport--Heilbronn theorem on zeros of certain Dirichlet series
nodes.statement: Earlier work of Davenport and Heilbronn \cite{dh1,dh2} established this result for the special case of the Hurwitz zeta-function $\zeta(s,\alpha)$ with rational parameter $\alpha$, and proved an analogue for the degree $2$ Epstein zeta-functions.
conclusions: established this result for the special case of the Hurwitz zeta-function $\zeta(s,\alpha)$ with rational parameter $\alpha$, and proved an analogue for the degree $2$ Epstein zeta-functions

nodes.name: Conrey--Ghosh theorem on zeros of the $L$-function of $\Delta^2$
nodes.statement: Also in degree $2$, Conrey and Ghosh \cite{cg} showed that the $L$-function associated to the square of Ramanujan's $\Delta$ modular form has infinitely many zeros outside of its critical strip.
conclusions: the $L$-function associated to the square of Ramanujan's $\Delta$ modular form has infinitely many zeros outside of its critical strip

nodes.name: Bombieri--Hejhal theorem on zeros of linear combinations of Euler products
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if we restrict to $\C$-linear combinations (i.e.\ homogeneous degree $1$ polynomials $P\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$) and $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$ with a common conductor and archimedean component $\pi_{1,\infty}\cong\ldots\cong\pi_{n,\infty}$, Bombieri and Hejhal \cite{bh} showed, subject to GRH and a weak form of the pair correlation conjecture for $L(s,\pi_j)$, that asymptotically $100\%$ of the non-trivial zeros of $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ have real part $\frac12$.
nodes.statement_short: Under GRH and pair correlation, almost all zeros of a linear combination of Euler products lie on $\Re(s)=\frac12$.
assumptions: if we restrict to $\C$-linear combinations (i.e.\ homogeneous degree $1$ polynomials $P\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$) and $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$ with a common conductor and archimedean component $\pi_{1,\infty}\cong\ldots\cong\pi_{n,\infty}$
subject to GRH and a weak form of the pair correlation conjecture for $L(s,\pi_j)$
conclusions: asymptotically $100\%$ of the non-trivial zeros of $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ have real part $\frac12$

nodes.name: Nakamura--Pa\'nkowski theorem on non-monomial polynomials of $L$-functions
nodes.statement: For instance, Nakamura and Pa\'nkowski \cite {np} have shown very recently, for a wide class of $L$-functions $L(s)$, that if $P\in R[x]$ is not a monomial and $\delta>0$ then $P(L(s))$ necessarily has zeros in the half-plane $\Re(s)>1-\delta$.
assumptions: for a wide class of $L$-functions $L(s)$
if $P\in R[x]$ is not a monomial and $\delta>0$
conclusions: $P(L(s))$ necessarily has zeros in the half-plane $\Re(s)>1-\delta$

nodes.name: Voronin's universality theorem
nodes.statement: Voronin \cite{voronin} proved for any compact set $K$ with connected complement contained within the strip $\Re(s) \in (\frac12, 1)$, and any nonvanishing, continuous function $f : K \rightarrow \C$ holomorphic on the interior of $K$, that $f$ can be uniformly approximated by vertical translates of the zeta function.
nodes.statement_short: Any nonvanishing holomorphic function on a compact subset of the strip is uniformly approximable by vertical shifts of $\zeta$.
assumptions: for any compact set $K$ with connected complement contained within the strip $\Re(s) \in (\frac12, 1)$, and any nonvanishing, continuous function $f : K \rightarrow \C$ holomorphic on the interior of $K$
conclusions: $f$ can be uniformly approximated by vertical translates of the zeta function

nodes.name: Laurin\v{c}ikas--Matsumoto joint universality theorem
nodes.statement: One result similar to ours, due to Laurin\v{c}ikas and Matsumoto \cite{LM}, states that given $m$ functions $f_1, \dots, f_m$ as above, and $L$-functions $L_j(s, F)$ associated to twists of a Hecke newform $F$ by pairwise inequivalent Dirichlet characters, that the $f_j$ may be simultaneously approximated by a single vertical translate of the functions $L_j(s, F)$. This implies \cite[Theorem 4]{LM} that non-trivial linear combinations of the $L_j(s, F)$ must contain zeros inside the critical strip with $\Re(s) > \frac{1}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Joint universality of twisted newform $L$-functions, implying their non-trivial linear combinations have zeros with $\Re(s)>\frac12$.
assumptions: given $m$ functions $f_1, \dots, f_m$ as above, and $L$-functions $L_j(s, F)$ associated to twists of a Hecke newform $F$ by pairwise inequivalent Dirichlet characters
conclusions: the $f_j$ may be simultaneously approximated by a single vertical translate of the functions $L_j(s, F)$
non-trivial linear combinations of the $L_j(s, F)$ must contain zeros inside the critical strip with $\Re(s) > \frac{1}{2}$

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1 (quasi-orthogonality of $\lambda_j(p)$ over arithmetic progressions)
nodes.statement: Let $a$ and $q$ be positive integers satisfying $\bigl(q,a\prod_{j=1}^n\cond(\pi_j)\bigr)=1$. Then \[ \sum_{\substack{p>y\\p\equiv{a}\;(\text{\rm mod }q)}} \frac{|u_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+u_n \lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma} = \bigg( \frac{1}{ \phi(q)} + O(\sigma-1)\bigg) \sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma} \] for all $y>0$, $\sigma\in(1,2]$ and all unit vectors $(u_1, \ldots, u_n)$, where the implied constant depends only on $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$ and $q$.
nodes.statement_short: Second moments of $\sum_j u_j\lambda_j(p)$ over a progression mod $q$ carry their expected share $1/\phi(q)$ of $\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}$.
assumptions: Let $a$ and $q$ be positive integers satisfying $\bigl(q,a\prod_{j=1}^n\cond(\pi_j)\bigr)=1$.
for all $y>0$, $\sigma\in(1,2]$ and all unit vectors $(u_1, \ldots, u_n)$
conclusions: \[ \sum_{\substack{p>y\\p\equiv{a}\;(\text{\rm mod }q)}} \frac{|u_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+u_n \lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma} = \bigg( \frac{1}{ \phi(q)} + O(\sigma-1)\bigg) \sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma} \]

nodes.name: Lemma 2.2 (neighborhood stability under $\GL_n(\C)$ action)
nodes.statement: Suppose $K$ is a compact subset of $\GL_n(\C)$, $g\in K$, and $U\subseteq\C^n$ contains an open $\delta$-neighborhood of some point. Then $gU$ contains an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood, where $\varepsilon > 0$ depends only on $\delta$ and $K$.
assumptions: Suppose $K$ is a compact subset of $\GL_n(\C)$, $g\in K$
$U\subseteq\C^n$ contains an open $\delta$-neighborhood of some point
conclusions: $gU$ contains an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood, where $\varepsilon > 0$ depends only on $\delta$ and $K$

nodes.name: Lemma 2.3 (square-root cancellation on average over phases)
nodes.statement: For any $v_0, \ldots, v_k \in \C^n$, there exist $\theta_0, \ldots, \theta_k \in [0, 1]$ such that \[ \left| \sum_{j = 0}^k e(\theta_k) v_j\right| \leq \sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^k|v_j|^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Phases can be chosen so that a sum of $k+1$ vectors has length at most the square root of the sum of their squared lengths.
assumptions: For any $v_0, \ldots, v_k \in \C^n$
conclusions: there exist $\theta_0, \ldots, \theta_k \in [0, 1]$ such that \[ \left| \sum_{j = 0}^k e(\theta_k) v_j\right| \leq \sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^k|v_j|^2}. \]

nodes.name: Lemma 2.4 (monomial criterion via the Nullstellensatz)
nodes.statement: Let $P\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Suppose that every solution to the equation $P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0$ satisfies $x_1\cdots x_n=0$. Then $P$ is a monomial, i.e., $P=cx_1^{d_1}\ldots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $c\neq0$ and non-negative integers $d_1,\ldots,d_n$.
nodes.statement_short: If the zero set of $P$ lies in the coordinate hyperplanes, then $P$ is a monomial.
assumptions: Let $P\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.
Suppose that every solution to the equation $P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0$ satisfies $x_1\cdots x_n=0$.
conclusions: $P$ is a monomial, i.e., $P=cx_1^{d_1}\ldots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $c\neq0$ and non-negative integers $d_1,\ldots,d_n$

nodes.name: Lemma 2.5 (continuity of zeros under perturbation of coefficients)
nodes.statement: Let $P\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and suppose that $y\in\C^n$ is a zero of $P$. Then for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that any polynomial $Q\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, obtained by changing any of the nonzero coefficients of $P$ by at most $\delta$ each, has a zero $z\in\C^n$ with $|y-z|<\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Zeros of a polynomial move continuously under small perturbations of its nonzero coefficients.
assumptions: Let $P\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and suppose that $y\in\C^n$ is a zero of $P$.
for any $\varepsilon>0$
conclusions: there exists $\delta>0$ such that any polynomial $Q\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, obtained by changing any of the nonzero coefficients of $P$ by at most $\delta$ each, has a zero $z\in\C^n$ with $|y-z|<\varepsilon$

nodes.name: Proposition 3.1 (simultaneous representation of $n$-tuples by tails of Euler products)
nodes.statement: For any real numbers $y,R>1$ there exists $\eta>0$ such that, for all $\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$, we have \begin{align*} \bigg\{\biggl(\prod_{p > y} L(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{j,p})\biggr)_{j=1,\ldots,n}&\ : t_p\in\R\text{ for each prime }p>y\bigg\}\\ &\supseteq \Big\{ (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \C^n : R^{-1} \leq |z_j| \leq R \textnormal{ for all } j \Big\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: With independent ordinates $t_p$, the tails $\prod_{p>y}L(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{j,p})$ realize every $n$-tuple of moduli in $[R^{-1},R]$.
assumptions: For any real numbers $y,R>1$
for all $\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \bigg\{\biggl(\prod_{p > y} L(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{j,p})\biggr)_{j=1,\ldots,n}&\ : t_p\in\R\text{ for each prime }p>y\bigg\}\\ &\supseteq \Big\{ (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \C^n : R^{-1} \leq |z_j| \leq R \textnormal{ for all } j \Big\}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proposition 3.2 (continuous solution of $\sum_i g_i f_i(z)=z$)
nodes.statement: Let \[ T = \{ (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \C^n \ : \ |z_1| = \ldots = |z_n| = 1 \}, \] \[ D = \{ (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \C^n \ : \ |z_1|, \ldots, |z_n| \leq 1 \}, \] and fix a compact set $K \subseteq \GL_n(\C)$. Then there is a number $m_0 > 0$ such that for every $m \geq m_0$ and all $(g_1, \ldots, g_m) \in K^m$, there are continuous functions $f_1, \ldots, f_m : D \rightarrow T$ such that $\sum_{i = 1}^m g_i f_i(z) = z$ for all $z \in D$.
nodes.statement_short: For enough matrices from a compact $K\subseteq\GL_n(\C)$, every $z\in D$ is continuously representable as $\sum_i g_i f_i(z)$ with $f_i$ valued in the torus $T$.
assumptions: Let \[ T = \{ (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \C^n \ : \ |z_1| = \ldots = |z_n| = 1 \}, \] \[ D = \{ (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \C^n \ : \ |z_1|, \ldots, |z_n| \leq 1 \}, \] and fix a compact set $K \subseteq \GL_n(\C)$.
conclusions: there is a number $m_0 > 0$ such that for every $m \geq m_0$ and all $(g_1, \ldots, g_m) \in K^m$, there are continuous functions $f_1, \ldots, f_m : D \rightarrow T$ such that $\sum_{i = 1}^m g_i f_i(z) = z$ for all $z \in D$

nodes.name: Proposition 3.3 (linearly independent twisted prime sums; construction of the compact set $K$)
nodes.statement: There is a compact set $K \subseteq \GL_n(\C)$, explicitly defined in \eqref{eqn:def_K} depending only on the degrees $r_1,\ldots,r_n$, with the following property: Let $m$ be a positive integer. Then there is a real number $\delta>0$ (depending on the $\pi_j$ and $m$) such that for any $y>0$ and any $\sigma\in(1,1+\delta]$, there exists a partition of $S(y)$ into $mn$ pairwise disjoint subsets $S_{ik}(y)$ ($i=1,\ldots,m$, $k=1,\ldots,n$) and a choice of $\epsilon_p \in S^1$ for each $p\in S(y)$, such that the $m$-tuple of matrices $(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$ defined by \begin{equation} g_i = \bigg( \frac{mn}{s(y,\sigma)} \sum_{p \in S_{ik}(y)} \frac{ \epsilon_p \lambda_j(p)}{p^{\sigma}} \bigg)_{1 \leq j, k \leq n}, \quad i=1,\ldots,m \end{equation} lies in $K^m$.
nodes.statement_short: One can partition the primes $p>y$ and twist by unimodular $\epsilon_p$ so that the resulting matrices $g_i$ all lie in a fixed compact subset of $\GL_n(\C)$.
assumptions: Let $m$ be a positive integer.
for any $y>0$ and any $\sigma\in(1,1+\delta]$
conclusions: there exists a partition of $S(y)$ into $mn$ pairwise disjoint subsets $S_{ik}(y)$ ($i=1,\ldots,m$, $k=1,\ldots,n$) and a choice of $\epsilon_p \in S^1$ for each $p\in S(y)$, such that the $m$-tuple of matrices $(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$ defined by \begin{equation} g_i = \bigg( \frac{mn}{s(y,\sigma)} \sum_{p \in S_{ik}(y)} \frac{ \epsilon_p \lambda_j(p)}{p^{\sigma}} \bigg)_{1 \leq j, k \leq n}, \quad i=1,\ldots,m \end{equation} lies in $K^m$

nodes.name: Compactness criterion in $\GL_n(\C)$
nodes.statement: We endow $\GL_n(\C)=\{g\in\Mat_{n\times n}(\C):\det{g}\ne0\}$ with the subspace topology. In particular, it is easy to see that a set $K\subseteq\GL_n(\C)$ is compact if and only if $K$ is closed in $\Mat_{n\times n}(\C)$ and there are positive real numbers $c$ and $C$ such that $$ \|g\|\le C\text{ and }|\det{g}|\ge c \quad\text{for all }g\in K. $$
nodes.statement_short: $K\subseteq\GL_n(\C)$ is compact iff it is closed with bounded Frobenius norm and determinant bounded away from $0$.
assumptions: We endow $\GL_n(\C)=\{g\in\Mat_{n\times n}(\C):\det{g}\ne0\}$ with the subspace topology.
conclusions: a set $K\subseteq\GL_n(\C)$ is compact if and only if $K$ is closed in $\Mat_{n\times n}(\C)$ and there are positive real numbers $c$ and $C$ such that $$ \|g\|\le C\text{ and }|\det{g}|\ge c \quad\text{for all }g\in K. $$

nodes.name: Boundedness of $\|g^{-1}\|$ on compact subsets of $\GL_n(\C)$
nodes.statement: Since $g^{-1}$ can be expressed in terms of $\frac1{\det{g}}$ and the cofactor matrix of $g$, it follows that $\|g^{-1}\|$ is bounded on $K$ (and indeed the map $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ is continuous, so that $\GL_n(\C)$ is a topological group with this topology).
nodes.statement_short: Inversion is continuous and $\|g^{-1}\|$ stays bounded on a compact $K$, so $\GL_n(\C)$ is a topological group.
assumptions: Since $g^{-1}$ can be expressed in terms of $\frac1{\det{g}}$ and the cofactor matrix of $g$
conclusions: $\|g^{-1}\|$ is bounded on $K$ (and indeed the map $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ is continuous, so that $\GL_n(\C)$ is a topological group with this topology)

nodes.name: Schwarz inequality for the Frobenius norm
nodes.statement: By the Schwarz inequality, we have $|Av|\le\|A\|\cdot|v|$ for any $A\in\Mat_{n\times n}(\C)$ and $v\in\C^n$.
assumptions: for any $A\in\Mat_{n\times n}(\C)$ and $v\in\C^n$
conclusions: $|Av|\le\|A\|\cdot|v|$

nodes.name: Generalized Ramanujan conjecture
nodes.statement: The generalized Ramanujan conjecture asserts that $|\alpha_{j,p,\ell}|\le 1$, with equality holding for all $p\nmid\cond(\pi_j)$, where $\cond(\pi_j)\in\Z_{>0}$ is the conductor of $\pi_j$. In particular, $|\lambda_j(p)|=|\alpha_{j,p,1}+\ldots+\alpha_{j,p,r_j}|\le r_j$.
nodes.statement_short: The local Satake parameters satisfy $|\alpha_{j,p,\ell}|\le1$, whence the Ramanujan bound $|\lambda_j(p)|\le r_j$.

nodes.name: Euler product for $L(s,\pi_j)$
nodes.statement: Each $\pi_j$ can be written as a restricted tensor product $\pi_{j,\infty}\otimes\bigotimes_p\pi_{j,p}$ of local representations, where $p$ runs through all prime numbers. Then we have \begin{equation} L(s,\pi_j)=\prod_pL(s,\pi_{j,p}),\quad\text{for }\Re(s)>1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $L(s,\pi_j)$ factors as an Euler product of local factors for $\Re(s)>1$.

nodes.name: Local factor $L(s,\pi_{j,p})$
nodes.statement: Here each local factor $L(s,\pi_{j,p})$ is a rational function of $p^{-s}$, of the form \begin{equation} L(s,\pi_{j,p})=\frac1{(1-\alpha_{j,p,1}p^{-s})\cdots(1-\alpha_{j,p,r_j}p^{-s})} \end{equation} for certain complex numbers $\alpha_{j,p,\ell}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each local factor is the reciprocal of a degree-$r_j$ polynomial in $p^{-s}$ with roots given by the Satake parameters.

nodes.statement_short: The representations satisfy the Ramanujan bound at all finite places and are pairwise non-isomorphic.

nodes.name: Remark 1 (monomial case, GRH rigidity)
nodes.statement: For $\pi_j$ as in the statement of the theorem, it is known (see \cite{jacquet-shalika}) that $L(s,\pi_j)$ does not vanish for $\Re(s)\ge1$. Thus if $P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ is a monomial then whether or not $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ vanishes for some $s$ with $\Re(s)>1$ is determined entirely by the finite Dirichlet series $D(s)$. Further, the Grand Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) predicts that each $L(s,\pi_j)$ does not vanish for $\Re(s)>\frac12$. Theorem~\ref{thm:main} demonstrates that the GRH, if it is true, is a very rigid phenomenon.
nodes.statement_short: In the monomial case zeros in $\Re(s)>1$ come only from $D(s)$; the theorem shows GRH is a rigid phenomenon.

nodes.name: Remark 2 (infinitely many zeros; comparison with Bombieri--Hejhal)
nodes.statement: By the almost-periodicity of Dirichlet series, if $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ has at least one zero with real part $>1$ then it must have infinitely many such zeros. In fact, our proof shows that there is some number $\eta=\eta(P;\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)>0$ such that for any $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ with $1<\sigma_1<\sigma_2\le1+\eta$, we have \begin{equation} \#\bigl\{s\in\C:\Re(s)\in[\sigma_1,\sigma_2], \Im(s)\in[-T,T], P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))=0\bigr\} \gg T \end{equation} for $T$ sufficiently large (where both the implied constant and the meaning of ``sufficiently large'' depend on $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ as well as $P$ and $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$). On the other hand, if we restrict to $\C$-linear combinations (i.e.\ homogeneous degree $1$ polynomials $P\in\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$) and $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$ with a common conductor and archimedean component $\pi_{1,\infty}\cong\ldots\cong\pi_{n,\infty}$, Bombieri and Hejhal \cite{bh} showed, subject to GRH and a weak form of the pair correlation conjecture for $L(s,\pi_j)$, that asymptotically $100\%$ of the non-trivial zeros of $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ have real part $\frac12$.
nodes.statement_short: One zero forces infinitely many, with a linear-in-$T$ count, yet under GRH almost all zeros still sit on the critical line.

nodes.name: Remark 3 (relaxing the Ramanujan assumption)
nodes.statement: The assumption of the Ramanujan conjecture in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} could be relaxed. For instance, it would suffice to have, for each fixed $j$: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)]some mild control over the coefficients of the logarithmic derivative $$\frac{L'}{L}(s,\pi_j)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty c_j(m)m^{-s}$$ at prime powers, namely $\sum_p\frac{|c_j(p^k)|^2}{p^k}<\infty$ for any fixed $k\ge2$ (cf.\ \cite[Hypothesis H]{rs}); \item[(ii)]an average bound for $|\lambda_j(p)|^4$ over arithmetic progressions of primes, namely $$ \limsup_{x\to\infty} \frac{\sum_{\substack{p\le x\\p\equiv a\;(\text{mod }q)}}|\lambda_j(p)|^4} {\sum_{\substack{p\le x\\p\equiv a\;(\text{mod }q)}}1} \le C_j, $$ for all co-prime $a,q\in\Z_{>0}$, where $C_j>0$ is independent of $a,q$. \end{itemize} Note that (i) is known to hold when $r_j\le 4$ (see \cite{rs,kim}). Further, both estimates follow from the Rankin--Selberg method if, for instance, the tensor square $\pi_j\otimes\pi_j$ is automorphic for each $j$. Since this is known when $r_j=2$ (see \cite{gj}), Theorem~\ref{thm:main} could be extended to include the $L$-functions associated to Maass forms.
nodes.statement_short: Ramanujan can be replaced by Hypothesis H plus a fourth-moment bound on progressions, covering Maass forms when $r_j=2$.

nodes.name: Remark 4 (quasi-orthogonality as the main tool; Selberg class)
nodes.statement: The main tool used in the proof is the quasi-orthogonality of the coefficients $\lambda_j(p)$, i.e.\ asymptotic estimates for sums of the form $\sum_{p\le x}\frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}}p$ as $x\to\infty$. These follow from the Rankin--Selberg method, and were obtained in a precise form independently by Wu--Ye \cite[Thm.~3]{wu-ye} and Avdispahi\'c--Smajlovi\'c \cite[Thm.~2.2]{as}. (We also make use of similar estimates for sums over $p$ in an arithmetic progression---see Lemma~\ref{lem:sump} for the exact statement---though it is likely that this could be avoided at the expense of making the proof more complicated.) Since quasi-orthogonality and the Ramanujan conjecture are essentially the only properties of automorphic $L$-functions that we require, one could instead take these as hypotheses and state the theorem for an axiomatically-defined class of $L$-functions, such as the Selberg class. However, it has been conjectured that the Selberg class coincides with the class of automorphic $L$-functions, so this likely offers no greater generality.
nodes.statement_short: Quasi-orthogonality (Rankin--Selberg) plus Ramanujan are the only inputs, so the result could be stated axiomatically for the Selberg class.

nodes.name: Remark 5 (the case $n=1$; comparison with Nakamura--Pa\'nkowski)
nodes.statement: The conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is interesting even for $n=1$. For instance, Nakamura and Pa\'nkowski \cite {np} have shown very recently, for a wide class of $L$-functions $L(s)$, that if $P\in R[x]$ is not a monomial and $\delta>0$ then $P(L(s))$ necessarily has zeros in the half-plane $\Re(s)>1-\delta$. Our result strengthens this to $\Re(s)>1$. (On the other hand, \cite{np} also yields the estimate \eqref{eqn:Nlowerbound} for any $[\sigma_1,\sigma_2]\subseteq(\frac12,1)$, which does not follow from our method.)
nodes.statement_short: Even for $n=1$ the theorem strengthens Nakamura--Pa\'nkowski from $\Re(s)>1-\delta$ to $\Re(s)>1$.

nodes.name: Remark 6 (relation to universality results)
nodes.statement: Our results are related to universality results for zeta and $L$-functions. Voronin \cite{voronin} proved for any compact set $K$ with connected complement contained within the strip $\Re(s) \in (\frac12, 1)$, and any nonvanishing, continuous function $f : K \rightarrow \C$ holomorphic on the interior of $K$, that $f$ can be uniformly approximated by vertical translates of the zeta function. Voronin's results were extended by a number of authors. One result similar to ours, due to Laurin\v{c}ikas and Matsumoto \cite{LM}, states that given $m$ functions $f_1, \dots, f_m$ as above, and $L$-functions $L_j(s, F)$ associated to twists of a Hecke newform $F$ by pairwise inequivalent Dirichlet characters, that the $f_j$ may be simultaneously approximated by a single vertical translate of the functions $L_j(s, F)$. This implies \cite[Theorem 4]{LM} that non-trivial linear combinations of the $L_j(s, F)$ must contain zeros inside the critical strip with $\Re(s) > \frac{1}{2}$. References to many more works on universality can be found in \cite{LM}.
nodes.statement_short: The results sit alongside Voronin-type universality and its joint extensions by Laurin\v{c}ikas--Matsumoto.

nodes.name: Erratum footnote to Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: [Added after publication.] As Mattia Righetti pointed out to us, this lemma is incorrect as claimed, although the statement is true with $O(\sigma - 1)$ replaced by $O\big( \frac{1}{\log(2/(\sigma - 1))}\big)$. The final line of the proof does not follow with the uniformity claimed, but in a published correction we prove that the bound $\sum_{p > y} p^{-\sigma} \gg \frac{y^{1 - \sigma}}{\log y} \log \frac{2}{\sigma - 1}$ does. The lemma is used in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:sw1}, where it is needed only that the error tend to $0$ as $\sigma \rightarrow 1^+$. The corrected error term is sufficient, and the remaining results remain valid with only cosmetic changes to the proofs.
nodes.statement_short: Post-publication correction: the error term must be weakened to $O(1/\log(2/(\sigma-1)))$, which still suffices for all downstream results.

nodes.name: Summary of the proof
nodes.statement: Our proof closely follows Saias and Weingartner's in broad outline, but becomes more technical in some places. The reader may wish to read \cite{SW} first. The technical heart of our paper is Proposition \ref{prop:lem2}, an extension of Lemma 2 of \cite{SW}. Given $n$ complex numbers $z_1, \cdots, z_n$ (bounded away from $0$ and $\infty$), we would like to simultaneously solve the equations $L(s, \pi_j) = z_j$, leading to a quick proof of the main theorem. As a substitute, we solve equations of a form $\prod_{p > y} L(\sigma + it_p, \pi_{j, p}) = z_j$, where the ordinate of $s$ is allowed to vary for each prime. Given this, in Section \ref{sec:main} we prove our main theorem, following the proof of Theorem 2 in \cite{SW}. As in \cite{SW}, the main tools are Weyl's criterion, allowing us to simultaneously approximate all of the $p^{-\sigma - it_p}$ by $p^{- \sigma - it}$ for a single $t$, and Rouch\'e's theorem, which states that actual zeros must exist near approximate zeros. The proof of Proposition \ref{prop:lem2} follows those of Lemmas 1 and 2 of \cite{SW}. However, in \cite{SW} the Dirichlet coefficients $\lambda(m)$ are all periodic to some fixed modulus, and this fact, combined with the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions, allows for easy control of various partial sums that need to be estimated. Here, we must do without this periodicity. To prove Proposition \ref{prop:lem2}, we choose (in Proposition \ref{prop:sw1}) a partition of the set of primes $p > y$ into disjoint subsets $S$, and complex numbers $\epsilon_p \in S^1$ for each $p > y$, so that the vectors of partial sums $\sum_{p \in S} \epsilon_p \lambda_j(p) p^{-\sigma}$ are linearly independent in a precise quantitative sense. Our main tool is the Rankin--Selberg method (substituting for periodicity and orthogonality of Dirichlet characters); see Lemma~\ref{lem:sump}. We also rely on the rather technical Proposition \ref{prop:td}, which says that for matrices $g_1, \dots, g_m$, we can continuously solve equations of the form $\sum_{i = 1}^m g_i f_i(z) = z$ for $n$-tuples of complex numbers $z = (z_1, \cdots, z_n)$. The $g_i$ are constructed from the sums over $p \in S$ considered in Proposition \ref{prop:sw1}, but we are able to formulate Proposition \ref{prop:td} in a general manner, without reference to automorphic forms or primes. The conclusion of Proposition \ref{prop:td} is guaranteed only for large $m$, so that the number of subsets $S$ needed may be large. We choose these subsets to be arithmetic progressions, for which the Rankin--Selberg estimates presented in Lemma \ref{lem:sump} are known to hold. If such estimates were unavailable, it seems likely that we could still obtain our result by constructing the $S$ in a more {\itshape ad hoc} fashion instead. In any case, and in contrast to Saias--Weingartner, the modulus of the arithmetic progression has no particular arithmetic significance, and is chosen to be coprime to all the conductors of the $\pi_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Roadmap: Proposition 3.1 replaces solving $L(s,\pi_j)=z_j$ by solving it with prime-dependent ordinates; Weyl and Rouch\'e then transfer this to genuine zeros.

nodes.name: Frobenius norm agrees with the Euclidean norm
nodes.statement: Note that this agrees with the Euclidean norm under the identification of $\Mat_{n\times n}(\C)$ with $\C^{n^2}$.

nodes.name: Interpretation of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: Loosely speaking, after simultaneously approximating the $t_p$ by a common $t$, it will follow that we can make the $L(s, \pi_j)$ independently approach any desired $n$-tuple of nonzero complex numbers, and this will allow us to find zeros in linear or polynomial combinations.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3.1 lets the $L(s,\pi_j)$ independently approach any nonzero target tuple, producing zeros of combinations.

nodes.name: Three-step outline of the proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: We will carry out the proof in three steps: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item We first show that there exist $\varepsilon > 0$ and $m_1$ such that for all $m \geq m_1$ and all $(g_1, \ldots, g_m) \in K^m$, the set $\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i : t_1,\ldots,t_m \in T \}$ contains an open $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of a point in $\C^n$. \item `Fattening' the neighborhood constructed in the first step, we will show that there exists $m_2$ such that for $m \geq m_2$ and all $(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in K^m$, $\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i : t_1,\ldots,t_m \in T \}$ contains the closed ball of radius $2$, $\{(z_1,\ldots,z_n):|z_1|^2+\ldots+|z_n|^2\le4\}$. \item Although the previous step yields a parametrization of a large closed set, it is not obviously continuous. By repeating the construction from step \eqref{it_small_neigh} using the added knowledge of step \eqref{it_big_neigh}, we show that one can achieve a continuous parametrization of $D$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The proof proceeds by producing a small neighborhood, fattening it to a ball of radius $2$, then making the parametrization continuous.

nodes.name: Motivation for Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: Next, we use the quasi-orthogonality of the coefficients $\lambda_j(p)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:sump}) to show that, by choosing an arbitrary ``twist'' $\epsilon_p\in S^1$ for each large prime $p$, we can make sums of the $\epsilon_p\lambda_j(p)$ line up in linearly independent directions, as quantified in the following proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting by unimodular $\epsilon_p$ turns quasi-orthogonality into linear independence of the prime sums.

nodes.name: Theorem 1.1 as a corollary of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: Our method is sufficiently general to apply to $L$-functions of all degrees, and in fact we obtain Theorem~\ref{thm:classical} as a corollary of the following general result:

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: Let $\chi\;(\text{mod }q)$ be a Dirichlet character, not necessarily primitive. We consider the sum \[ E_{jk\chi}(x)= \sum_{p\le x}\big(\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p) -\delta_{jk\chi}\big)\frac{\log{p}}{p}, \] running over primes $p\le x$, where $\delta_{jk\chi}=1$ if $j=k$ and $\chi$ is the trivial character, and $0$ otherwise. Applying \cite[(2) and (3)]{as} with $(\pi,\pi')=(\pi_j\otimes\chi,\pi_k)$ and, if $\chi$ is imprimitive, subtracting any contribution from the terms with $p|q$, we obtain the bound $E_{jk\chi}(x)\ll_q 1$. Next, for any non-integral $y\ge\frac32$ and any $\sigma\in(1,2]$, we have $$ \sum_{p>y} \frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)-\delta_{jk\chi}}{p^\sigma} =\int_y^\infty\frac{t^{1-\sigma}}{\log{t}}\,dE_{jk\chi}(t). $$ Integrating by parts and applying the above estimate for $E_{jk\chi}$, we see that this is $\ll_q y^{1-\sigma}/\log{y}$. Now, expanding the square and using orthogonality of Dirichlet characters, we have $$ \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{p>y\\p\equiv{a}\;(\text{mod }q)}} \frac{|u_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+u_n\lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma}&= \frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{\chi\;(\text{mod }q)}u_j\overline{u_k}\overline{\chi(a)} \sum_{p>y}\frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)}{p^\sigma}\\ &=O_q\!\left(\frac{y^{1-\sigma}}{\log{y}}\right) +\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}. \end{aligned} $$ Finally, by the prime number theorem we have $\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}\gg\frac{y^{1-\sigma}}{(\sigma-1)\log{y}}$, uniformly for $y\ge\frac32$ and $\sigma\in(1,2]$. The lemma follows.
nodes.statement_short: Selberg-orthogonality estimates for $E_{jk\chi}(x)$ plus partial summation and character orthogonality, closed by the prime number theorem.

nodes.name: Introduce the weighted prime sum $E_{jk\chi}(x)$
nodes.statement: Let $\chi\;(\text{mod }q)$ be a Dirichlet character, not necessarily primitive. We consider the sum \[ E_{jk\chi}(x)= \sum_{p\le x}\big(\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p) -\delta_{jk\chi}\big)\frac{\log{p}}{p}, \] running over primes $p\le x$, where $\delta_{jk\chi}=1$ if $j=k$ and $\chi$ is the trivial character, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Define the twisted Rankin--Selberg partial sum $E_{jk\chi}(x)$.

nodes.name: Bound $E_{jk\chi}(x)$ via Selberg orthogonality
nodes.statement: Applying \cite[(2) and (3)]{as} with $(\pi,\pi')=(\pi_j\otimes\chi,\pi_k)$ and, if $\chi$ is imprimitive, subtracting any contribution from the terms with $p|q$, we obtain the bound $E_{jk\chi}(x)\ll_q 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke the Selberg-orthogonality estimates of \cite{as} to get $E_{jk\chi}(x)\ll_q 1$.

nodes.name: Partial summation to a tail estimate
nodes.statement: Next, for any non-integral $y\ge\frac32$ and any $\sigma\in(1,2]$, we have $$ \sum_{p>y} \frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)-\delta_{jk\chi}}{p^\sigma} =\int_y^\infty\frac{t^{1-\sigma}}{\log{t}}\,dE_{jk\chi}(t). $$ Integrating by parts and applying the above estimate for $E_{jk\chi}$, we see that this is $\ll_q y^{1-\sigma}/\log{y}$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts to bound the tail by $y^{1-\sigma}/\log y$.

nodes.name: Expand the square and use character orthogonality
nodes.statement: Now, expanding the square and using orthogonality of Dirichlet characters, we have $$ \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{p>y\\p\equiv{a}\;(\text{mod }q)}} \frac{|u_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+u_n\lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma}&= \frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{\chi\;(\text{mod }q)}u_j\overline{u_k}\overline{\chi(a)} \sum_{p>y}\frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)}{p^\sigma}\\ &=O_q\!\left(\frac{y^{1-\sigma}}{\log{y}}\right) +\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}. \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Detect the progression with characters, isolating the main term $\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}$.

nodes.name: Compare error to main term by the prime number theorem
nodes.statement: Finally, by the prime number theorem we have $\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}\gg\frac{y^{1-\sigma}}{(\sigma-1)\log{y}}$, uniformly for $y\ge\frac32$ and $\sigma\in(1,2]$. The lemma follows.
nodes.statement_short: Use the PNT lower bound for $\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}$ to convert the error into $O(\sigma-1)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: By linearity, we may assume without loss of generality that $U$ contains the $\delta$-neighborhood of the origin, $N_\delta$. Since $K$ is compact, there is a number $C>0$ such that $\|g^{-1}\|\le C$ for all $g\in K$. Put $\varepsilon=C^{-1}\delta$, and let $N_\varepsilon$ be the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the origin. For any $v\in N_\varepsilon$ we have $|g^{-1}v|\le\|g^{-1}\|\cdot|v|<C\varepsilon=\delta$, so that $v=g(g^{-1}v)\in gN_\delta$. Since $v$ was arbitrary, $gN_\delta\supseteq N_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize to the origin and take $\varepsilon=C^{-1}\delta$ with $\|g^{-1}\|\le C$ on the compact $K$.

nodes.name: Reduce to a neighborhood of the origin
nodes.statement: By linearity, we may assume without loss of generality that $U$ contains the $\delta$-neighborhood of the origin, $N_\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Use linearity to place the $\delta$-neighborhood at the origin.

nodes.name: Choose $C$ and set $\varepsilon=C^{-1}\delta$
nodes.statement: Since $K$ is compact, there is a number $C>0$ such that $\|g^{-1}\|\le C$ for all $g\in K$. Put $\varepsilon=C^{-1}\delta$, and let $N_\varepsilon$ be the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the origin.
nodes.statement_short: Extract a uniform bound $\|g^{-1}\|\le C$ from compactness and define $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Verify $gN_\delta\supseteq N_\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: For any $v\in N_\varepsilon$ we have $|g^{-1}v|\le\|g^{-1}\|\cdot|v|<C\varepsilon=\delta$, so that $v=g(g^{-1}v)\in gN_\delta$. Since $v$ was arbitrary, $gN_\delta\supseteq N_\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: We have \[ \int_{[0, 1]^k}\left|\sum_{j=0}^k e(\theta_j) v_j\right|^2 d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_k = \sum_{j=0}^{k}|v_j|^2. \] Thus, the average choice of $(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k)$ satisfies the conclusion.
nodes.statement_short: Averaging over phases gives $\sum_j|v_j|^2$ exactly, so some choice of phases does at least as well.

nodes.name: Compute the mean square over phases
nodes.statement: We have \[ \int_{[0, 1]^k}\left|\sum_{j=0}^k e(\theta_j) v_j\right|^2 d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_k = \sum_{j=0}^{k}|v_j|^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality of characters gives the exact mean-square identity.

nodes.name: Pass from average to a single choice
nodes.statement: Thus, the average choice of $(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k)$ satisfies the conclusion.
nodes.statement_short: Some phase vector attains at most the average value.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\C^n:P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\}$ be the vanishing set of $P$. By hypothesis, the polynomial $x_1\cdots x_n$ vanishes on $V$. Thus, since $\C$ is algebraically closed, Hilbert's Nullstellensatz implies that there is some $d\in\Z_{\ge0}$ such that $(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$ is contained in the ideal generated by $P$, i.e.\ $P|(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$. Since $\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is a unique factorization domain, this is only possible if $P$ is a monomial.
nodes.statement_short: Nullstellensatz gives $P\mid(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$, and unique factorization forces $P$ to be a monomial.

nodes.name: Introduce the vanishing set $V$
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\C^n:P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\}$ be the vanishing set of $P$. By hypothesis, the polynomial $x_1\cdots x_n$ vanishes on $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up $V=Z(P)$ and note $x_1\cdots x_n$ vanishes on it.

nodes.name: Apply Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
nodes.statement: Thus, since $\C$ is algebraically closed, Hilbert's Nullstellensatz implies that there is some $d\in\Z_{\ge0}$ such that $(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$ is contained in the ideal generated by $P$, i.e.\ $P|(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$.
nodes.statement_short: Nullstellensatz yields $P\mid(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$.

nodes.name: Conclude by unique factorization
nodes.statement: Since $\C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is a unique factorization domain, this is only possible if $P$ is a monomial.
nodes.statement_short: UFD property forces $P$ to divide a monomial, hence be one.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.5
nodes.statement: If $P$ is identically $0$ then so is $Q$, so we may take $z=y$. Otherwise, set $$ p(t)=P(y+tu)\quad\text{and}\quad q(t)=Q(y+tu) $$ for $t\in\C$, where $u$ is any unit vector for which $p(t)$ does not vanish for all $t$; shrinking $\varepsilon$ if necessary, assume that $p(t)$ does not vanish on $C_\varepsilon=\{t\in\C:|t|=\varepsilon\}$; and let $\gamma>0$ be the minimum of $|p(t)|$ on $C_\varepsilon$. For $t\in C_\varepsilon$ we have \[ |q(t) - p(t)| < \delta N \Big(1+\varepsilon+|y|\Big)^{\deg P} \] where $N$ is the number of nonzero coefficients of $P$. Choosing $\delta$ so that the right side of this expression is bounded by $\gamma$, we have $|q(t)-p(t)|<|p(t)|$ for $t\in C_\varepsilon$. By Rouch\'e's theorem $q(t)$ has a zero $t_0$ of modulus $|t_0|<\varepsilon$, and taking $z=y+t_0u$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to a complex line through $y$ and apply Rouch\'e's theorem on the circle $C_\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Dispose of the case $P\equiv0$
nodes.statement: If $P$ is identically $0$ then so is $Q$, so we may take $z=y$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial case: $P\equiv0$.

nodes.name: Restrict to a line and set up $p,q,\gamma$
nodes.statement: Otherwise, set $$ p(t)=P(y+tu)\quad\text{and}\quad q(t)=Q(y+tu) $$ for $t\in\C$, where $u$ is any unit vector for which $p(t)$ does not vanish for all $t$; shrinking $\varepsilon$ if necessary, assume that $p(t)$ does not vanish on $C_\varepsilon=\{t\in\C:|t|=\varepsilon\}$; and let $\gamma>0$ be the minimum of $|p(t)|$ on $C_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict $P,Q$ to a line through $y$ and take $\gamma=\min_{C_\varepsilon}|p|$.

nodes.name: Bound $|q-p|$ on the circle
nodes.statement: For $t\in C_\varepsilon$ we have \[ |q(t) - p(t)| < \delta N \Big(1+\varepsilon+|y|\Big)^{\deg P} \] where $N$ is the number of nonzero coefficients of $P$. Choosing $\delta$ so that the right side of this expression is bounded by $\gamma$, we have $|q(t)-p(t)|<|p(t)|$ for $t\in C_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\delta$ making the coefficient perturbation smaller than $\gamma$.

nodes.name: Apply Rouch\'e's theorem
nodes.statement: By Rouch\'e's theorem $q(t)$ has a zero $t_0$ of modulus $|t_0|<\varepsilon$, and taking $z=y+t_0u$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Rouch\'e produces a nearby zero of $Q$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: We begin by showing \eqref{it_small_neigh}. By compactness, there is an $m_1$ such that for any $m\ge m_1$ and any $m$-tuple $(g_1, \ldots, g_m)$, there is a distinct pair of indices $i,j$ such that $\| g_i^{-1} g_j - I \| < \frac{1}{3 \sqrt{n}}$. Assume, without loss of generality, that $(i,j)=(1,2)$, and put $\Delta = g_1^{-1} g_2 - I$. Then for any choice of $t_1, t_2 \in T$, we have \[ g_1 t_1 + g_2 t_2 = g_1 (t_1 + (I + \Delta) t_2), \] where $\| \Delta \|<\frac1{3\sqrt{n}}$. We introduce some notation. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: Let $q$ be the smallest prime number satisfying $q\equiv1\pmod{mn}$ and $q\nmid\prod_{j=1}^n\cond(\pi_j)$. We put $t=\frac{q-1}{mn}$ and define $S_{ik}^\circ(y)$ to be the union of residue classes $$ S_{ik}^\circ(y)=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^t \bigl\{p\in S(y):p\equiv tn(i-1)+t(k-1)+\ell\pmod{q}\bigr\}, $$ and $$ S_{ik}(y)=\begin{cases} S_{ik}^\circ(y)\cup\{q\}&\text{if } i=k=1\text{ and }y<q,\\ S_{ik}^\circ(y)&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ Then the $S_{ik}(y)$ are pairwise disjoint and cover $S(y)$. For a fixed choice of $i$, let $v_k$ denote the $k$th column of $g_i$, as defined in \eqref{eqn:gidef}, with the $\epsilon_p$ yet to be chosen. We will show by induction that there is a choice of the $\epsilon_p$ such that \begin{equation} |v_\ell - \proj_{\textspan\{v_1, \ldots, v_{\ell - 1}\}} v_\ell| \geq \frac{1}{2r} \end{equation} holds for every $\ell=1,\ldots,n$, where $r=\sqrt{r_1^2+\ldots+r_n^2}$. To that end, let $k$ be given, and assume that \eqref{eqn:projspan} has been established for $\ell=1,\ldots,k-1$. Choose a unit vector $u = (u_1, \ldots, u_n)$ orthogonal to $v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}$. By the Schwarz inequality and the Ramanujan bound $|\lambda_j(p)|\le r_j$, for each prime $p$ we have $ |\bar{u}_1 \lambda_1(p) + \ldots + \bar{u}_n \lambda_n(p)| \leq r. $ Therefore \begin{align} \frac{mn}{s(y, \sigma)} \sum_{p\in S_{ik}(y)} \frac{|\bar{u}_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+\bar{u}_n\lambda_n(p)|}{p^\sigma} &\geq\frac{mn}{r s(y, \sigma)} \sum_{p\in S_{ik}^\circ(y)} \frac{|\bar{u}_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+\bar{u}_n\lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma}\\ &=\frac{1+O_{m, n}(\sigma-1)}{r}, \nonumber \end{align} the latter equality following by Lemma \ref{lem:sump}. We choose $\delta$ so that the $O$ term above is bounded in modulus by $\frac12$, and for each $p \in S_{ik}(y)$ we choose $\epsilon_p$ such that $\epsilon_p (\bar{u}_1 \lambda_1(p) + \ldots + \bar{u}_n \lambda_n(p))$ is real and nonnegative. Then the left side of \eqref{eqn:inn_prod} equals \[ \langle u, v_k \rangle = \langle u, v_k - \proj_{\textspan\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}\}} v_k \rangle \leq |v_k - \proj_{\textspan\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}\}} v_k|, \] so that \eqref{eqn:projspan} follows for $\ell=k$. Applying Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization to $v_1,\ldots,v_n$, it follows from \eqref{eqn:projspan} that $|\det{g_i}|\ge (2r)^{-n}$. Moreover, by the Schwarz inequality and Lemma \ref{lem:sump} again, each entry of $g_i$ is bounded above by $1+O_{m, n}(\sigma-1)$, so that $\|g_i\|\le2n$ for a suitable choice of $\delta$. Thus, \begin{equation} K=\{g\in\GL_n(\C):\|g\|\le 2n, |\det{g}|\ge(2r)^{-n}\} \end{equation} has the desired properties.
nodes.statement_short: Partition the primes into residue classes mod an auxiliary prime $q$, then choose the twists $\epsilon_p$ inductively so each new column of $g_i$ sticks out of the previous span.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: We use Propositions \ref{prop:sw1} and \ref{prop:td} to determine a compact set $K\subseteq\GL_n(\C)$, a positive integer $m_0$, and a real number $\delta>0$ with the properties described there. Taking $m=m_0$, the aforementioned propositions yield, for any $\sigma\in(1,1+\delta]$, an $m$-tuple of matrices $(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in K^m$, elements $\epsilon_p \in S^1$ for each prime $p > y$, and continuous functions $f_1,\dots,f_m:D\rightarrow T$ such that \begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^m g_i f_i(z) = z\quad\text{for all }z\in D. \end{equation} Now, let $\mu=\frac{s(y,\sigma)}{mn}$. For each prime $p>y$, we define a continuous function $t_p : \mu D\rightarrow\R$ satisfying \begin{equation} p^{- i t_p(z)} = \epsilon_p f_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k, \end{equation} where $(i,k)$ is the unique pair of indices for which $p\in S_{ik}(y)$ and $f_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k$ denotes the $k$th component of $f_i(\mu^{-1}z)$. (Note that the lift from $S^1$ to $\R$ is possible since $D$ is simply connected.) Define an error term $E(z)=(E_1(z),\ldots,E_n(z))$ by writing, for each $j=1,\ldots,n$, $$ E_j(z)=\sum_{p>y}\left(\log L(\sigma+it_p(z),\pi_{j,p}) -\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}\right). $$ By the Ramanujan bound, we have $$ \log L(s,\pi_{j,p})-\lambda_j(p)p^{-s}=O(p^{-2}) $$ uniformly for $\Re(s)\ge1$. Since $\sum_p p^{-2}$ converges, the continuity of $E$ follows from that of the individual $t_p$. Moreover, each component $E_j(z)$ is bounded by a number $C>0$, independent of $j$, $z$, $y$, or $\sigma$. Set $R'=\sqrt{\pi^2+\log^2{R}}$. We take $\eta\in(0,\delta]$ small enough that the condition $\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$ ensures that $\mu\ge C+R'$. By \eqref{eqn:id_decomp}, \eqref{eqn:def_tp}, and Proposition \ref{prop:sw1} we have $$ \sum_{p>y}\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}= \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{p\in S_{ik}(y)} \frac{\lambda_j(p)\epsilon_pf_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k}{p^{\sigma}}=z_j, $$ for any $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mu{D}$. Now fix $w\in R'D$ and define a function $F_w:(C+R')D\to\C$ by $F_w(z)=w-E(z)$. By the estimate for $E_j(z)$ above, the image of $F_w$ is contained in $(C+R')D$. Thus, by the Brouwer fixed point theorem, there exists $z\in(C+R')D$ with $F_w(z)=z$, so that \[ \biggl(\sum_{p>y}\log L(\sigma+it_p(z),\pi_{j,p})\biggr)_{j=1,\ldots,n} =z+E(z)=z+w-F_w(z)=w. \] Taking exponentials yields the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Feed Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 into a Brouwer fixed-point argument for $F_w(z)=w-E(z)$, then exponentiate the resulting logarithmic identity.

nodes.name: Define $\mu$ and the ordinates $t_p(z)$
nodes.statement: Now, let $\mu=\frac{s(y,\sigma)}{mn}$. For each prime $p>y$, we define a continuous function $t_p : \mu D\rightarrow\R$ satisfying \begin{equation} p^{- i t_p(z)} = \epsilon_p f_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k, \end{equation} where $(i,k)$ is the unique pair of indices for which $p\in S_{ik}(y)$ and $f_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k$ denotes the $k$th component of $f_i(\mu^{-1}z)$. (Note that the lift from $S^1$ to $\R$ is possible since $D$ is simply connected.)
nodes.statement_short: Lift the unimodular values $\epsilon_pf_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k$ to real ordinates $t_p(z)$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Bound the error term $E(z)$
nodes.statement: Define an error term $E(z)=(E_1(z),\ldots,E_n(z))$ by writing, for each $j=1,\ldots,n$, $$ E_j(z)=\sum_{p>y}\left(\log L(\sigma+it_p(z),\pi_{j,p}) -\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}\right). $$ By the Ramanujan bound, we have $$ \log L(s,\pi_{j,p})-\lambda_j(p)p^{-s}=O(p^{-2}) $$ uniformly for $\Re(s)\ge1$. Since $\sum_p p^{-2}$ converges, the continuity of $E$ follows from that of the individual $t_p$. Moreover, each component $E_j(z)$ is bounded by a number $C>0$, independent of $j$, $z$, $y$, or $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\log L-\lambda_j(p)p^{-s}=O(p^{-2})$, so $E$ is continuous and bounded by $C$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Identify the linear part with $z_j$
nodes.statement: Set $R'=\sqrt{\pi^2+\log^2{R}}$. We take $\eta\in(0,\delta]$ small enough that the condition $\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$ ensures that $\mu\ge C+R'$. By \eqref{eqn:id_decomp}, \eqref{eqn:def_tp}, and Proposition \ref{prop:sw1} we have $$ \sum_{p>y}\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}= \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{p\in S_{ik}(y)} \frac{\lambda_j(p)\epsilon_pf_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k}{p^{\sigma}}=z_j, $$ for any $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mu{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\sum_{p>y}\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}$ as $z_j$ using the partition.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Brouwer fixed point and exponentiation
nodes.statement: Now fix $w\in R'D$ and define a function $F_w:(C+R')D\to\C$ by $F_w(z)=w-E(z)$. By the estimate for $E_j(z)$ above, the image of $F_w$ is contained in $(C+R')D$. Thus, by the Brouwer fixed point theorem, there exists $z\in(C+R')D$ with $F_w(z)=z$, so that \[ \biggl(\sum_{p>y}\log L(\sigma+it_p(z),\pi_{j,p})\biggr)_{j=1,\ldots,n} =z+E(z)=z+w-F_w(z)=w. \] Taking exponentials yields the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: A fixed point of $F_w(z)=w-E(z)$ yields the prescribed value $w$; exponentiate.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: The proof will be carried out in two steps: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item Applying our previous results, we show that unless $P$ is a monomial (as described in Theorem \ref{thm:main}), for every $\sigma > 1$ sufficiently close to $1$ there are real numbers $t_p$ (for each prime $p$) and $t_0$ such that $P|_{s=\sigma+it_0}$ vanishes at $\bigl(\prod_pL(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{1,p}),\ldots, \prod_pL(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{n,p})\bigr)$. \item Simultaneously approximating the $p^{-it_p}$ by $p^{-it}$ for a common value of $t$, we use Rouch\'e's theorem to find a zero of $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ close to $\sigma+it$. \end{enumerate} Note that the second step is standard and is applied in \cite{SW} in much the same way. \\ \\ We begin with a polynomial $P$ whose coefficients are finite Dirichlet series $D(s)=\sum_{m=1}^M a_mm^{-s}$, and let $y$ be the largest value of $M$ occurring in any of these coefficients. We rewrite each $L(s,\pi_j)$ as $L_{\leq{y}}(s,\pi_j)L_{>y}(s,\pi_j)$, splitting each Euler product into products over primes $p\leq y$ and $p>y$ respectively. Setting $$ Q(x_1,\ldots,x_n) =P\bigl(L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_1)x_1,\ldots,L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_n)x_n\bigr), $$ we have $P(L(s,\pi_1),\dots,L(s,\pi_n))=Q(L_{>y}(s,\pi_1),\dots,L_{>y}(s,\pi_n))$. The coefficients of $Q$ are rational functions of the $p^{-s}$ for $p\le y$. More precisely, for any monomial term $D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ in the expansion of $P$, the corresponding term of $Q$ is \[D(s)L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_1)^{d_1}\cdots{}L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_n)^{d_n} x_1^{d_1}\cdots{}x_n^{d_n}. \] Since the finite Euler products $L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_j)$ are non-vanishing holomorphic functions on $\{s\in\C:\Re(s)\ge1\}$, the corresponding terms of $P$ and $Q$ have the same zeros there. Let $D_1(s),\ldots,D_m(s)$ run through the coefficients of $P$ which do not vanish identically, and consider their product $f(s)=D_1(s)\cdots D_m(s)$. Then $f$ is itself a finite Dirichlet series which does not vanish identically. By complex analysis, $f$ cannot vanish at $1+it$ for every $t\in\R$, so there is some $t_0$ for which $D_1(1+it_0),\ldots,D_m(1+it_0)$ are all non-zero, and the same holds for the corresponding terms of $Q$. Next we specialize the coefficients of $Q$ to a fixed value of $s$, obtaining a polynomial $h_s\in\C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. Considering $s=1+it_0$, Lemma \ref{lem:monomial} implies that either $h_{1+it_0}=cx_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $c\in\C$ and $d_1,\ldots,d_n\in\Z_{\ge0}$, or that there are $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\C$, none zero, for which $h_{1+it_0}(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=0$. In the former case, it follows from our choice of $t_0$ that $P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ is a monomial, as allowed in the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Henceforth we assume that we are in the latter case, and aim to show that $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ has a zero with $\Re(s)>1$. We choose $R>1$ so that $R^{-{1/2}}\leq|y_j|\leq R^{1/2}$ for every $j$. By Lemma \ref{lem:poly_cont}, there is a number $\varepsilon>0$ such that for every $\sigma\in(1,1+\varepsilon]$, there exists $(z_1(\sigma),\ldots,z_n(\sigma))\in\C^n$ satisfying $h_{\sigma+it_0}(z_1(\sigma),\ldots,z_n(\sigma))=0$ and $R^{-1}\leq|z_j(\sigma)|\leq R$ for every $j$. We use Proposition \ref{prop:lem2} to determine $\eta$ in terms of $y$ and $R$, and assume that $\eta \le \varepsilon$ by shrinking $\eta$ if necessary. Proposition~\ref{prop:lem2} then guarantees that, for every $\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$, we can solve the simultaneous system of equations $$ \prod_{p>y}L(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{j,p})=z_j(\sigma),\quad j=1,\ldots,n, $$ in the $t_p$ for $p>y$. For $p\le y$ we set $t_p=t_0$, thereby completing step (1). \\ \\ Turning to step (2), let $\sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\R$ with $1<\sigma_1<\sigma_2\le1+\eta$, and put $\sigma=\frac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}2$. With the $t_0$ and $t_p$ resulting from step (1) for this choice of $\sigma$, let $P_{it_0}$ denote the polynomial obtained from $P$ by replacing $s$ by $s+it_0$ in all of its coefficients, and define \begin{equation} F(s)=P_{it_0}\!\left( \prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{1,p}),\ldots,\prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{n,p})\right). \end{equation} Then $F$ is holomorphic for $|s-\sigma|<\sigma-1$ and satisfies $F(\sigma)=0$ by construction. It follows that there is a number $\rho\in(0,\frac{\sigma_2-\sigma_1}2]$ such that $F(s)\neq0$ for all $s\in C_\rho=\{s\in\C:|s-\sigma|=\rho\}$. Write $\gamma$ for the minimum of $|F(s)|$ on $C_\rho$. Next, by abuse of notation, we write $P(s)$ as shorthand for $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$. As $P(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty a_mm^{-s}$ converges absolutely as a Dirichlet series for $\Re(s) > 1$, there is an integer $M > 0$ with $\sum_{m=M}^{\infty}|a_m|m^{-\sigma_1}\le\frac{\gamma}3$. By \eqref{eqn:Fdef} we have $F(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty b_mm^{-s}$, where $b_m=a_m\prod_{p|m}p^{-it_p\ord_p(m)}$, and by the joint uniform distribution of $p^{it}$ for primes $p<M$, it follows that the set of $t\in\R$ satisfying \[\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}\frac{|a_mm^{-it}-b_m|}{m^{\sigma_1}}<\frac{\gamma}3\] has positive lower density. For any such $t$ the triangle inequality yields $|P(s+it)-F(s)|<\gamma$ for all $s$ with $\Re(s)\ge\sigma_1$, and in particular for all $s\in C_\rho$. By Rouch\'e's theorem, it follows that $P(s+it)$ has a zero $s$ with $|s-\sigma|<\rho$. Thus, $P(s)$ has zeros with real part in $[\sigma_1,\sigma_2]$, and indeed we have $$ \#\{s\in\C:\Re(s)\in[\sigma_1,\sigma_2], \Im(s)\in[-T,T], P(s)=0\} \gg_{\sigma_1,\sigma_2}T $$ for all $T\ge T_0(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the Euler products at $y$, use Lemma 2.4 to force a nonzero zero of the specialized polynomial, realize it by Proposition 3.1, then transfer to a true zero by uniform distribution and Rouch\'e's theorem.

nodes.name: Split the Euler products at $y$ and define $Q$
nodes.statement: We begin with a polynomial $P$ whose coefficients are finite Dirichlet series $D(s)=\sum_{m=1}^M a_mm^{-s}$, and let $y$ be the largest value of $M$ occurring in any of these coefficients. We rewrite each $L(s,\pi_j)$ as $L_{\leq{y}}(s,\pi_j)L_{>y}(s,\pi_j)$, splitting each Euler product into products over primes $p\leq y$ and $p>y$ respectively. Setting $$ Q(x_1,\ldots,x_n) =P\bigl(L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_1)x_1,\ldots,L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_n)x_n\bigr), $$ we have $P(L(s,\pi_1),\dots,L(s,\pi_n))=Q(L_{>y}(s,\pi_1),\dots,L_{>y}(s,\pi_n))$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $L=L_{\le y}L_{>y}$ and absorb the finite part into a new polynomial $Q$.

nodes.name: Coefficients of $Q$ have the same zeros as those of $P$
nodes.statement: The coefficients of $Q$ are rational functions of the $p^{-s}$ for $p\le y$. More precisely, for any monomial term $D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ in the expansion of $P$, the corresponding term of $Q$ is \[D(s)L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_1)^{d_1}\cdots{}L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_n)^{d_n} x_1^{d_1}\cdots{}x_n^{d_n}. \] Since the finite Euler products $L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_j)$ are non-vanishing holomorphic functions on $\{s\in\C:\Re(s)\ge1\}$, the corresponding terms of $P$ and $Q$ have the same zeros there.
nodes.statement_short: The finite Euler factors are nonvanishing on $\Re(s)\ge1$, so zeros are unchanged.

nodes.name: Choose $t_0$ with all coefficients nonzero at $1+it_0$
nodes.statement: Let $D_1(s),\ldots,D_m(s)$ run through the coefficients of $P$ which do not vanish identically, and consider their product $f(s)=D_1(s)\cdots D_m(s)$. Then $f$ is itself a finite Dirichlet series which does not vanish identically. By complex analysis, $f$ cannot vanish at $1+it$ for every $t\in\R$, so there is some $t_0$ for which $D_1(1+it_0),\ldots,D_m(1+it_0)$ are all non-zero, and the same holds for the corresponding terms of $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: The product of the nonzero coefficients cannot vanish on the whole line $\Re(s)=1$.

nodes.name: Monomial dichotomy via Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement: Next we specialize the coefficients of $Q$ to a fixed value of $s$, obtaining a polynomial $h_s\in\C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. Considering $s=1+it_0$, Lemma \ref{lem:monomial} implies that either $h_{1+it_0}=cx_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $c\in\C$ and $d_1,\ldots,d_n\in\Z_{\ge0}$, or that there are $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\C$, none zero, for which $h_{1+it_0}(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=0$. In the former case, it follows from our choice of $t_0$ that $P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ is a monomial, as allowed in the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Henceforth we assume that we are in the latter case, and aim to show that $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ has a zero with $\Re(s)>1$.
nodes.statement_short: Either $h_{1+it_0}$ is a monomial (done) or it has a zero with all coordinates nonzero.

nodes.name: Realize the approximate zero by Proposition 3.1, completing step (1)
nodes.statement: We choose $R>1$ so that $R^{-{1/2}}\leq|y_j|\leq R^{1/2}$ for every $j$. By Lemma \ref{lem:poly_cont}, there is a number $\varepsilon>0$ such that for every $\sigma\in(1,1+\varepsilon]$, there exists $(z_1(\sigma),\ldots,z_n(\sigma))\in\C^n$ satisfying $h_{\sigma+it_0}(z_1(\sigma),\ldots,z_n(\sigma))=0$ and $R^{-1}\leq|z_j(\sigma)|\leq R$ for every $j$. We use Proposition \ref{prop:lem2} to determine $\eta$ in terms of $y$ and $R$, and assume that $\eta \le \varepsilon$ by shrinking $\eta$ if necessary. Proposition~\ref{prop:lem2} then guarantees that, for every $\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$, we can solve the simultaneous system of equations $$ \prod_{p>y}L(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{j,p})=z_j(\sigma),\quad j=1,\ldots,n, $$ in the $t_p$ for $p>y$. For $p\le y$ we set $t_p=t_0$, thereby completing step (1).
nodes.statement_short: Perturb the zero by Lemma 2.5, then solve $\prod_{p>y}L(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{j,p})=z_j(\sigma)$.

nodes.name: Step (2): define $F$ and the circle $C_\rho$ with $\gamma=\min|F|$
nodes.statement: Turning to step (2), let $\sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\R$ with $1<\sigma_1<\sigma_2\le1+\eta$, and put $\sigma=\frac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}2$. With the $t_0$ and $t_p$ resulting from step (1) for this choice of $\sigma$, let $P_{it_0}$ denote the polynomial obtained from $P$ by replacing $s$ by $s+it_0$ in all of its coefficients, and define \begin{equation} F(s)=P_{it_0}\!\left( \prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{1,p}),\ldots,\prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{n,p})\right). \end{equation} Then $F$ is holomorphic for $|s-\sigma|<\sigma-1$ and satisfies $F(\sigma)=0$ by construction. It follows that there is a number $\rho\in(0,\frac{\sigma_2-\sigma_1}2]$ such that $F(s)\neq0$ for all $s\in C_\rho=\{s\in\C:|s-\sigma|=\rho\}$. Write $\gamma$ for the minimum of $|F(s)|$ on $C_\rho$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $F$ from the prime-dependent ordinates, vanishing at $\sigma$, and isolate $\gamma>0$.

nodes.name: Approximate by a single $t$ and apply Rouch\'e
nodes.statement: Next, by abuse of notation, we write $P(s)$ as shorthand for $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$. As $P(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty a_mm^{-s}$ converges absolutely as a Dirichlet series for $\Re(s) > 1$, there is an integer $M > 0$ with $\sum_{m=M}^{\infty}|a_m|m^{-\sigma_1}\le\frac{\gamma}3$. By \eqref{eqn:Fdef} we have $F(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty b_mm^{-s}$, where $b_m=a_m\prod_{p|m}p^{-it_p\ord_p(m)}$, and by the joint uniform distribution of $p^{it}$ for primes $p<M$, it follows that the set of $t\in\R$ satisfying \[\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}\frac{|a_mm^{-it}-b_m|}{m^{\sigma_1}}<\frac{\gamma}3\] has positive lower density. For any such $t$ the triangle inequality yields $|P(s+it)-F(s)|<\gamma$ for all $s$ with $\Re(s)\ge\sigma_1$, and in particular for all $s\in C_\rho$. By Rouch\'e's theorem, it follows that $P(s+it)$ has a zero $s$ with $|s-\sigma|<\rho$. Thus, $P(s)$ has zeros with real part in $[\sigma_1,\sigma_2]$, and indeed we have $$ \#\{s\in\C:\Re(s)\in[\sigma_1,\sigma_2], \Im(s)\in[-T,T], P(s)=0\} \gg_{\sigma_1,\sigma_2}T $$ for all $T\ge T_0(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Joint uniform distribution of $p^{it}$ makes $P(s+it)$ within $\gamma$ of $F$, so Rouch\'e gives genuinely many zeros.
